newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - CSR profit plunges, but sees upturn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CSR profit plunges, but sees upturn.

text.p: Building materials, aluminium and sugar group CSR reported its worst annual result in four years and warned that it did not plan to invest much more funds in its core Australian building materials due to the subdued outlook.
The profit was described as "totally inadequate" by managing director Geoffrey Kells.

But CSR, Australia's largest listed building materials group, said it expected a profit upturn in the year to March 31, 1998, on the back of a long awaited turnaround in the country's housing industry and continued growth in its U.S. business.

CSR earlier reported a 36 percent drop in net profit after abnormals to A$212.2 million in 1996/97, which was well within market expectations. Sales dipped slightly to A$6.126 billion from its operations in Australia, Asia and the United States.
The Sydney-based group blamed the local housing market, which has recently showed signs of renewed life after being in a depressed state since mid-1994.
However, CSR expected a better year ahead.
"The outlook for the year ahead is more favourable than for the year just completed," CSR said in a statement accompanying its 1996/97 results.
A modest recovery is expected in Australian building and construction activity, together with healthy levels of activity in the United States market, CSR said.
But export returns from raw sugar and aluminium will be lower, unless markets improve from current levels, it said.

The 1996/97 profit represented a return of 7.9 percent on funds employed before abnormal items, its worst performance since 1993. CSR has over A$7.79 billion in assets and has spend about A$2.0 billion on its businesses in the past two years.
"We accept that the profit performance is totally inadequate," Kells said. Analysts said the result was within expectations, but it may lead to a pruning of 1997/98 forecasts.
CSR's 1997/98 pre-abnormal net profits are forecast between A$290 million and A$320 million.
Kells said further profit growth will come from existing assets, although about A$100 million worth of assets, mainly in Australia, are marked for sale.
He said profit from its core Australian construction and building materials businesses will come from further cost cutting, modest price rises and the expected housing upturn.

However, the Australian construction and building materials business was unlikely to get further significant investment, due to the subdued outlook for the sector, Kells said. "As to Australia, we do see very little opportunity," he said.

"It is one of the consequences of certain fundamental characteristics of the Australian manufacturing industry, the Australian immigration policy, the ageing Australian population, the trends in housing," he said.
"We do see continuing growth opportunities in America, that is what we have been doing and specific add-on opportunities will be sought in Asia," he said.
Kells said Asian expansion would be aided through its alliance with the Kuok group headed by Malaysian businessman Robert Kuok.
CSR shares closed steady at A$4.76.
